Neonates of the fairy shrimp Chirocephalus ruffoi emerge from resting eggs with a total body length of merely 0.07 cm [Lb = 0.07 cm] at birth, placing them among the smallest anostracan hatchlings described. This minute size at the onset of the free-swimming larval phase imposes substantial constraints on their early feeding ecology, as nauplius larvae must immediately commence filter feeding on suspended particles to fuel rapid growth. The initial dry weight at this stage, calculated from the egg diameter of 0.301 mm, is a meager 0.00000265 grams , reflecting the finite yolk reserves allocated during embryogenesis. Such limited endogenous resources dictate that exogenous food items must be encountered without delay, and field observations confirm that the first feeding event typically occurs within hours of hatching. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this combination of short initial body length and extremely low birth weight represents a conserved life-history strategy among temporary-pond anostracans, balancing investment in egg production against the survival probability of larvae in ephemeral habitats.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], Chirocephalus ruffoi individuals achieve an ultimate total length of 1.65 cm [Li = 1.65 cm], a size that is modest even by branchiopod standards. This asymptotic body length appears to be reached after a growth period of several weeks, with the post-metamorphic juvenile phase characterized by a steady increase in body segment number and appendage differentiation. The corresponding ultimate dry weight at this terminal size is 0.0076 grams , a value that scales allometrically from measurements in related anostracans. Interestingly, the ratio of final dry mass to total length in this species indicates a slightly more slender body form compared to certain Artemia populations, possibly as an adaptation to reduce metabolic costs during the prolonged, cold-water conditions of its alpine vernal pool habitats. Repeated measurements of mature adults confirm that this maximum size is rarely exceeded, suggesting a strong genetic or physiological constraint on growth cessation.

Reproductive output in Chirocephalus ruffoi has been quantified through detailed laboratory rearing experiments at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], revealing a maximum brood size of 93.7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 93.7 eggs per clutch], with an interbrood interval of 7.7 days, corresponding to approximately 47 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 47 clutches per year]. These two components together define the species' capacity for rapid population increase under favorable conditions. The production of such large clutches places a significant energetic burden on the ovigerous female, which must balance the demands of egg maturation against its own somatic maintenance requirements. Field surveys in temporary ponds corroborate the laboratory findings, though natural broods tend to be slightly smaller, likely due to resource limitation or predation pressure on adults. This high fecundity, combined with the capacity for producing dormant resting eggs, allows the species to persist in environments where the hydroperiod may vary dramatically from year to year. The interval between reproductive events is notably short for an anostracan inhabiting a cold-water system.

Sexual maturation in Chirocephalus ruffoi proceeds rapidly when individuals are reared at an elevated temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], with the time since birth at puberty recorded as 18 days [tp = 18 days]. This accelerated developmental trajectory is typical of species adapted to ephemeral water bodies, where a premium is placed on early reproduction before habitat desiccation. At the onset of puberty, individuals measure approximately 0.72 cm [Lp = approximately 0.72 cm] in total length, a size that marks the transition from the growing juvenile stage to the reproductively active adult phase. The relatively modest length at puberty suggests that this species allocates a substantial portion of its growth to reproductive structures early in life, rather than deferring maturation until a larger body size is attained. In contrast, individuals maintained at cooler temperatures, such as the 13 °C [T = 13 °C] used in longevity studies, show a markedly slower pace of development, although the precise age at puberty under those thermal conditions has not been experimentally determined.

The lifespan of Chirocephalus ruffoi under controlled conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] is 79 days [am = 79 days], a duration that aligns closely with the typical hydroperiod of its alpine vernal pool habitats. This relatively short maximum longevity, combined with the rapid attainment of sexual maturity described above, defines a classic "fast" life-history strategy typical of inhabitants of highly seasonal environments. Older individuals, particularly those approaching the end of their lifespan, often exhibit a decline in feeding activity and a progressive deterioration of thoracic appendage function, culminating in natural mortality. The ultimate dry weight of 0.0076 grams  recorded in fully grown adults represents the peak of somatic investment, after which little further growth occurs. Comparisons with other branchiopod species inhabiting temporary waters suggest that the total length at birth of 0.07 cm [Lb = 0.07 cm] combined with a lifespan of just over two and a half months represents an adaptive package that maximizes the probability of completing at least one generation before the pond dries.
